newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian opposition win may mean more reform delay.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian opposition win may mean more reform delay.

text.p: Defeat for Bulgaria's governing Socialists in Sunday's first round of presidential elections will increase pressure for early parliamentary polls.
But analysts say crucial economic reforms may now face fresh delays while the government and opposition establish a new balance of power.

Preliminary official results from Sunday's voting showed Petar Stoyanov of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) with 43.65 percent, comfortably ahead of the Socialists' Ivan Marazov, who had 27.07 percent.
"It's a resounding defeat for Marazov, he seems to have attracted only the hardcore Socialist vote," said one Sofia-based diplomat.

After communist ruler Todor Zhivkov was toppled in 1989, his party colleagues hastily renamed themselves the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) and stunned the West by winning parliamentary elections the following year.

This time round, many Socialist votes went to George Ganchev, the clownish head of the Bulgarian Business Bloc, who won 22.18 percent and gave a ranting, incoherent Sunday night news conference at which he heaped abuse on both main parties.
"It's a huge protest vote, but this is the sort of thing that happens in a country where people have lost their way politically and don't understand what's happening to them," the diplomat said.
Many of the 6.75 million electorate simply did not vote. Sunday's estimated turnout of 60 percent was much lower than the 75 percent recorded for the 1994 parliamentary elections.

Delays in implementing market reforms have dragged Bulgaria deep into economic crisis. An International Monetary Fund mission arrives on Wednesday for more talks on release of a twice-delayed $115 million credit, vital if Bulgaria is to avoid default on its foreign debt.
Shortages loom in the coming Balkan winter as the central bank struggles to stretch dwindling reserves to prop up the local currency and buy fuel and wheat.
While other ex-Soviet satellites woo foreign investors and press for membership of NATO and the European Union, Bulgaria clings stubbornly to the last vestiges of its communist past.
IMF-prescribed privatisations and the closure of loss-making state companies are held up by pressure from powerful vested interests.

Forecasts of negative growth and 240 percent inflation for 1996 offer no glimmer of hope. Record high interest rates introduced to stabilise the collapsing banking system have doubled internal debt since the start of the year.
Political analyst Miroslav Popov, a member of the BSP ruling council, said a win for the liberal pro-market Stoyanov would not necessarily help to resolve the economic crisis.
"Stoyanov's election as a president will mean further instability in the country which will result in yet another delay for the reforms," he said.
The results show a big change in Bulgarian voting patterns, with the anti-communist vote consolidating around the UDF, while former Socialist voters desert the party.
The outcome of Sunday's second round may depend on how Ganchev's supporters vote. His small party usually backs the Socialists in parliament but he has ruled out any deals with either candidate.

The government of Prime Minister Zhan Videnov has a secure majority in parliament but a Stoyanov win is expected to prompt more soul-searching within the BSP, whose divisions have become more public since the October 2 killing of former prime minister Andrei Lukanov.

Most analysts say cabinet changes are on the cards but an early general election would require a parliamentary vote of no confidence, and few commentators expect the Socialists effectively to vote themselves out of office in the immediate future.
"I think they will keep on squabbling and keep on attempting to govern, at least for a while," said one diplomat.
